And when a distant supernova explodes, its entire light curve runs in slow motion by exactly the same factor as its spectral redshift, as if the universe stretched both the light’s color and the event’s ticking clock together. All these independent clues point to motion and cosmic expansion, not to static stars conveniently choosing red paint.

Short answer: no. Even a flawless, perfectly shaped, impossibly large glass lens can’t “see” atoms with visible light. The roadblock isn’t craftsmanship, it’s physics. Light behaves like ripples, and you can’t use big ripples to draw tiny details—like trying to paint eyelashes with a broom. Visible light waves are about 400–700 nanometers long, and the smallest detail a lens can resolve is on the order of half a wavelength. That sets a best-case limit of roughly 200 nanometers, while atoms are about 0.1 nanometers across—thousands of times smaller. You can always magnify the blur, but you can’t pull out details the light never carried.

To see atoms you must either use much shorter “ripples” or skip light altogether. Electron microscopes use electrons, whose wave-like behavior has a wavelength tiny compared to atomic sizes, so they can resolve individual columns of atoms. X-rays also have suitably short wavelengths, though focusing them is tricky, so special optics are used. Another route is to “feel” the surface instead of looking: scanning tunneling and atomic force microscopes trace atoms the way a blind person reads Braille, building up images from touch rather than light.

There are clever optical tricks that push past the usual limit—ultraviolet light, “super‑resolution” fluorescence, or near‑field methods—but these get you down to tens of nanometers, not to the scale of atoms. So a perfect magnifying glass can’t do it; different waves or different senses are required.

Short answer: no. A black hole’s “edge” isn’t a lid you can lever up; it’s a boundary in spacetime—the point of no return where even light can’t find a path out. Bringing in a second black hole doesn’t open a crack; it tilts the playing field even more steeply inward. Picture two waterfalls rushing together: the currents don’t cancel to reveal dry ground—they join to make a bigger, more inescapable plunge.

When two black holes get close, their boundaries can stretch and wobble, but then a single, larger boundary quickly forms around both, sealing everything inside. There’s a built-in rule of gravity that, classically, the total “surface” of this boundary can only grow, not shrink, so no temporary window appears. You can shake energy out of a spinning black hole’s outskirts or hear the pair ring space like a bell via gravitational waves, but none of that exposes the interior. The only known way a black hole “opens” is the glacial leak of Hawking radiation, and that’s more like ice sublimating than a door swinging wide. Speculative ideas about wormholes would need exotic negative-energy stuff we’ve never seen. So a crowbar made of another black hole just makes a bigger lock.

Think of a planet transit as a small, perfectly round coin sliding across a lamp, and a starspot as a smudge on the lamp’s surface. In the brightness record, a planet makes a tidy, clockwork shadow: a brief, symmetric dip that repeats at precisely the same intervals with nearly the same depth and duration each time. Starspots ride along with the star’s rotation, so they make slow, lumpy dimmings that change shape and timing as spots grow, fade, and migrate. In Kepler data, transits look like neat “U”-shaped bites lasting a few hours and returning on a strict schedule, while starspot signals are broader, often wavy modulations over days that drift and evolve. Scientists also fit the dip with a transit geometry model; if the width, depth, and timing don’t add up to a physically plausible orbit around a star of the measured size, it’s not a planet.

Color and follow-up checks add extra certainty. A planet blocks light regardless of color, so the dip depth is nearly the same in red and infrared as in visible light, whereas a cool starspot is darker in blue than in red, making a color-dependent dimming. When possible, astronomers observe the same event in different colors or with infrared telescopes to test this. They also look for the star’s tiny “wobble” from the planet’s pull; a true planet produces a matching, regular tug, while spots mainly just add noise. Ironically, sometimes you even see little bumps inside the dip—caused when the planet crosses over a dark spot and briefly blocks less light—which is a telltale signature that a real planet is passing in front of a blotchy stellar surface rather than the blotch itself causing the dip.

Most computer monitors are LCDs: a very thin sandwich of layers with a soft “liquid crystal” filling between sheets, plus a light behind it. In normal use, those crystals act like tiny, twistable blinds that steer the light so each pixel looks the right color and brightness. When you press the screen, you squeeze and tilt that soft middle layer and slightly bend the surrounding sheets. The crystals no longer twist the light the way the electronics intend, so the spot you press lets through the “wrong” amount or direction of light. It looks fluid because, at this scale, those molecules really do behave like a liquid and relax back into place after you let go.

The shimmering colors or bull’s‑eye rings you sometimes see are a bonus effect, like rainbows on an oil slick. Pressing changes the thickness and tension of several ultra-thin films in the stack. White light bouncing and passing through these layers interferes with itself, and different colors get boosted or canceled depending on the exact spacing—so you see bands of color that spread like ripples on a pond. When the pressure is removed, the layers flatten, the crystals re‑align, and the picture returns to normal. Press hard or often enough, though, and you can bruise pixels or delaminate layers, leaving a permanent mark—so it’s best to admire the “liquid” trick sparingly.

There is a difference between “having an antiderivative” and “having an antiderivative you can write with the usual symbols.” Every continuous function does have an antiderivative: you can always define F(x) = ∫_0^x f(t) dt. That F exists, can be computed numerically, and can be plotted—so graphs are no problem. What sometimes fails is finding a tidy formula built from the familiar building blocks (polynomials, exponentials, logs, sines, cosines, and a finite number of additions, multiplications, and compositions). Graphing is like taking snapshots point by point; finding a closed-form antiderivative is like asking for a one-sentence poem that describes the whole landscape. Many landscapes don’t fit in a sentence.

Why can’t we always find such a sentence? Because the “elementary” toolbox is small, and differentiation tends to stay inside it while integration often escapes it. Think of differentiation as a conveyor belt that turns Lego creations into other Lego-friendly shapes; running the belt backward (integration) can produce shapes that no combination of your Lego bricks can build. Mathematicians have made this precise: theorems and algorithms (like Liouville’s theorem and the Risch algorithm) prove that functions such as sin(x)/x and sin(x^2) do not have elementary antiderivatives. So we give their integrals new names—Si(x) for ∫ sin(x)/x dx, and the Fresnel integrals for ∫ sin(x^2) dx—and treat them as perfectly good “special functions.” For x^x, the antiderivative also isn’t elementary, but we can define F(x) = ∫_0^x t^t dt and compute or graph it just fine. In short: the road exists and is drivable; it just doesn’t have a simple street name.

Carbon dioxide is used because, when its level rises, it acts a bit like a fast “sleep switch” for the brain. CO2 dissolves into the blood, makes it more acidic, and that acidity has an anesthetic-like effect that quickly blunts awareness before the heart and breathing stop. It’s inexpensive, nonflammable, easy to supply and contain, and—when the concentration is raised gradually—animals typically lose consciousness before the most unpleasant sensations peak. For those practical and welfare reasons, many veterinary and research guidelines have accepted CO2 as a standard method, even while acknowledging it isn’t perfect.

Nitrogen and nitric oxide don’t offer that same built‑in anesthetic cushion. Pure nitrogen simply removes oxygen; it’s like being taken to high altitude in a sealed elevator—your body’s alarm for “air hunger” can kick in before you black out, which is distressing. Nitric oxide is worse: in air it forms nitrogen dioxide, a harsh lung irritant that can cause burning injury to the airways, making it both inhumane for animals and hazardous to people nearby. If you meant nitrous oxide (laughing gas), it’s too weak on its own to reliably cause unconsciousness and death, and using it by creating low‑oxygen conditions still brings back that air‑hunger problem. So, while there’s active debate and ongoing refinement to reduce aversion, CO2 remains common because it can produce rapid loss of consciousness when applied properly and is practical to implement safely.

Short answer: if the box says “ibuprofen 200 mg” (or 400 mg), the pain‑relieving ingredient is the same whether it’s a pricey brand like Nurofen or the store brand. Regulators require generics to work just as well as brands. Think of it like cars with the same engine under different paint jobs—the look and marketing may differ, but the power under the hood is the same. What can differ are the “extras”: coatings, liquid‑gel capsules (which may kick in a bit faster for some people), taste, or packaging. Branding can also create a placebo boost—your brain sometimes gives the expensive box extra credit.

When is it worth paying more? If you specifically want a fast‑dissolving liquid gel, need a certain form that’s easier to swallow, or you’re avoiding an added ingredient. Otherwise, the cheaper plain ibuprofen is usually the best value. Watch out for “targeted” or “for back pain/migraine” versions that are just regular ibuprofen at a higher price, and avoid combo products unless you need the extras (some add decongestants or, in some countries, codeine). Use the lowest effective dose (commonly 200–400 mg every 6–8 hours, max 1,200 mg/day over the counter), take with food if it upsets your stomach, and check with a pharmacist or clinician if you have stomach ulcers, kidney or heart problems, are on blood thinners, or are pregnant.

Short answer: there isn’t one single “fat gene” that dooms someone to gain weight. A few rare, single-gene glitches can cause severe, early-onset obesity by powerfully driving hunger and lowering energy use—like a broken thermostat stuck on “heat.” More commonly, one gene called FTO was nicknamed the “fat gene” because certain versions are linked to slightly higher body weight, but even that effect is modest on its own.

For most people, body weight is shaped by hundreds of genes, each nudging appetite, satiety, how rewarding food feels, and how the body stores energy—think of a soundboard with many tiny sliders rather than one big on/off switch. Twin and family studies suggest that these sliders explain a notable share of differences in body size (roughly 40–70%), but the environment is the amplifier: abundant, tasty calories, stress, poor sleep, and low movement can turn small genetic nudges into larger changes on the scale. In other words, genes set the range, and the world we live in helps decide where within that range we land. Genetics isn’t destiny, but it does mean the same lifestyle can be easier for some bodies than others—more like running with a tailwind for some and a headwind for others.

A reactor’s power comes from a self-sustaining chain of splits in the fuel, much like a campfire fed by logs and kept alive by flying sparks. If you don’t replace the “logs” (fissile atoms), two things happen at once: the pile of burnable fuel slowly shrinks, and the “ash” from burning (certain fission fragments) builds up and soaks up the “sparks” (neutrons). With fewer good logs and more ash in the way, the fire naturally wants to settle down; left entirely alone, the chain reaction would weaken and the power would drift downward over time.

In real reactors, operators counter this gradual weakening by backing out control rods and making other adjustments, effectively fanning the fire so it stays at the desired heat. That works for many months because the core is loaded with some extra reactivity at the start. But there’s a limit: eventually all the “fan” is used up—control rods are mostly out and chemistry tweaks are maxed—so the highest power the core can sustain begins to “coast down.” Plants then run at slowly decreasing output until the reactor can no longer hold the target power and must be shut down for refueling. Typical light‑water reactors maintain full power for much of a 12–24 month cycle, then spend weeks at a gently falling output before refueling restores the “fresh logs” and clears out the “ash.”

Think of scent as a faint newspaper carried on the wind. From far away, dogs and cats can catch the headline—something interesting is over there—but the ink gets thinner with distance and breeze. Up close, the “print” is darker and more detailed. Many of the clues they care about—who left the scent, what they ate, how long ago—live in heavier, oily molecules stuck to skin, soil, or grass. Those don’t float far. To read that biography rather than just the headline, they press their noses to the source, like using a magnifying glass on fine print.

Getting close also lets their equipment work best. They sniff in quick bursts, taking many tiny samples, and each nostril samples slightly different air, a bit like stereo hearing for smell. The shape of their nose sends fresh air in and pushes used air out to the sides, which helps lift new odor molecules off a surface—imagine blowing gently on dust to make it rise and then catching it. Their noses are moist to trap scent particles, and cats may even pull certain smells into a second smell organ in the roof of the mouth to analyze social signals. Up close, all these tools turn a vague whiff into a detailed map.
